Name: knowledge_provenance_probe
Title: Where Did You Learn That? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Encode the Provenance and Reliability of Their Facts
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM stores a fact, it also implicitly encodes a separable signal about *how well* and *from what kind of source* it learned that fact (frequently-attested vs. rarely-seen, consistent vs. contradicted-in-training). We hypothesize that this 'provenance/reliability' signal is (1) linearly decodable from internal activations at retrieval time, (2) distinct from both the fact content and the model's output logit confidence, and (3) causally responsible for whether the model defers, hedges, or overrides its stored answer when a query invites doubt. In short: LLMs partially know *how well they know* a fact, and that meta-signal is a distinct, readable, steerable internal quantity.
Related Work: Prior calibration work (Kadavath et al. 2022 'know what they know', semantic entropy, P(True)) probes uncertainty behaviorally or via output logits but does not localize a provenance signal in activations distinct from content. Mechanistic recall work (Geva et al. 2023; Fierro et al. 2024; Hochman et al. 2026) dissects *where* a fact is stored but not whether *reliability metadata* is co-stored. Sycophancy/knowledge-conflict work (Yu et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2025) studies when models override stored knowledge behaviorally without a mechanistic reliability variable. Our contribution is the first study to (a) construct facts with controlled, known training provenance (via injection during continued pretraining/fine-tuning with logged frequency and consistency) and matched natural facts, (b) test whether a linear direction encodes reliability separately from content and from output confidence, and (c) causally intervene on that direction to change hedging/deferral behavior. No prior work isolates a co-stored, steerable provenance representation.
Abstract: Language models sometimes state facts flatly, sometimes hedge, and sometimes defer to a user's correction—but it is unclear whether these behaviors are driven by an internal representation of how reliably a fact was learned, or merely by surface output statistics. We investigate whether LLMs co-store a *provenance/reliability* signal alongside factual content: an internal, decodable estimate of how well-attested a fact was during training. To gain ground truth over provenance, we continue-train small open models on synthetic corpora in which we log, for each injected fact, its occurrence frequency, source diversity, and whether it was contradicted by conflicting statements. We then probe, at retrieval time, whether a linear direction in the residual stream predicts a fact's true reliability class, and critically whether this direction is *separable* from (i) the fact's content direction and (ii) the model's output-logit confidence—ruling out the trivial explanation that reliability is just calibrated logits. Using activation patching and directional steering, we test whether manipulating the reliability direction causally changes the model's tendency to hedge, express uncertainty, or accept a user's correction, while holding the retrieved answer fixed. We further test whether the same reliability probe, trained on synthetic facts, transfers to natural facts (predicting Wikidata-frequency and known-hallucination-prone items). Experiments use Pythia and Qwen2.5 at multiple scales. This yields the first evidence for (or against) a co-stored, readable, and steerable notion of epistemic provenance inside language models, with direct implications for hallucination detection and controllable hedging.
Experiments: 1) SYNTHETIC PROVENANCE CORPUS: Create a set of ~2k fictional entity-attribute facts (novel names/attributes to avoid pretraining leakage). Assign each fact to a provenance condition by controlling how it appears in a continued-training corpus: (a) HIGH-RELIABILITY = high frequency, many paraphrased sources, no contradictions; (b) LOW-FREQUENCY = appears a few times; (c) CONTRADICTED = appears with conflicting alternate answers; (d) SINGLE-SOURCE = frequent but from one templated source. Continue-train Pythia (410M/1.4B) and Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B) on this corpus mixed with generic text. Verify each fact is learned (recall accuracy) so we analyze only stored facts. 2) PROVENANCE PROBE: At the answer position during recall, train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to predict the provenance class; report accuracy on held-out facts and identify best layers. 3) SEPARABILITY TESTS: (i) Content separability—check that the provenance probe still works after projecting out the answer-token content direction, and that provenance and content directions are near-orthogonal. (ii) Logit-confidence separability—show provenance predicts reliability class *beyond* output entropy/max-logit (incremental accuracy over a logit-only baseline; partial correlation). 4) CAUSAL STEERING: Extract the difference-of-means direction between HIGH and LOW/CONTRADICTED reliability. At inference, add/subtract it (scaled by alpha) at the answer position while holding the query fixed, and measure behavioral change: hedging-phrase rate, expressed-uncertainty markers, and acceptance rate when a user asserts a wrong correction. Confirm the retrieved answer token is unchanged when possible (isolating meta-signal from content). Baselines: random-direction steering, content-direction steering. 5) NATURAL-FACT TRANSFER: Apply the synthetic-trained provenance probe (or a small recalibration) to a set of natural facts stratified by Wikidata frequency and by membership in known hallucination-prone sets; test whether predicted reliability correlates with real recall accuracy and hallucination rate (AUROC for predicting incorrect answers). 6) SCALING: Compare probe accuracy, separability, and steering efficacy across scales. METRICS: probe accuracy per class, orthogonality/partial correlation with content and logits, incremental AUROC over logit baseline, causal steering effect sizes on hedging/deferral, natural-fact hallucination-prediction AUROC, scaling trends.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The provenance signal might be inseparable from output-logit confidence, which would be a negative-but-informative result; we design explicit separability tests rather than assume separation. 2) Continued-training on synthetic facts may induce artifacts (e.g., templated surface cues); we mitigate with paraphrase diversity and by testing transfer to natural facts. 3) Linear-probe decodability may reflect a probe artifact, not a used signal; the causal steering experiment is the key test that the direction is functional. 4) Steering the reliability direction may inadvertently alter content; we measure answer-token stability and treat content-preserving steering as the success criterion. 5) Small models may not have learned rich provenance encoding; we scale up as feasible and report the scale at which the signal emerges. 6) Natural-fact 'frequency' is a noisy proxy for training provenance since we lack access to the base pretraining corpus; we treat this as a coarse validity check, not ground truth.
